question: The Swedish Government has proposed (SOU 2025:99) a special law to allow the general withdrawal of permanent residence permits, which would be replaced by temporary residence permits. Concerns have been raised about the proposal’s compatibility with EU law and human rights.

Under Council Directive 2003/109/EC, permanent residence permits may only be withdrawn under specific conditions: serious offences, threats to public policy or public security, or fraud and abuses in the application process. If those criteria are not met, Member States do not have the right to withdraw the permit.

At the same time, Article 7 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) protects the right to private and family life. Restrictions may be imposed only if they are in accordance with the law, necessary and proportionate with regard to the objective pursued. The withdrawal of permanent residence permits may therefore affect that right. Questions: 1.
On the basis of Council Directive 2003/109/EC, how does the Commission assess Sweden’s proposal to withdraw permanent residence permits?
What are the consequences for a country that breaches the directive?
How does the Commission ensure that national rules meet the requirements of necessity and proportionality under Article 7 of the ECHR?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.1.2026) The status of permanent or long-term resident can be regulated by national or EU law. In the latter case, Council Directive 2003/109/EC on the status of third-country nationals who are long-term residents (the ‘Long-Term Residents Directive’)1 applies.

The Directive regulates the conditions for granting and withdrawing the status of long-term resident and the rights pertaining thereto. The provisions of the Directive only apply to third-country nationals who hold a long-term residence permit under the terms of the Directive, and not to all thirdcountry nationals holding a permanent residence permit issued under national law.
The Commission does not comment on draft proposals or political programme. However, the Commission will monitor the situation and follow up with the concerned Member State, if relevant.
